fixes.explanation: That's the reason the text gives: “…for what has been decreed must be accomplished.” He will be successful until the time of wrath is completed, and not a day past it. He does as he pleases, but he's still working on a clock he didn't set.

The text never says the other kings are afraid of him. What it says is that he will be successful until the time of wrath is completed, “…for what has been decreed must be accomplished.” So his success has an end point, the completing of the time of wrath. That decree is the reason the text gives.

No valleys in this verse, friend. The god he honors in place of the others is “…a god of fortresses…” and it's a god his fathers did not know. The gifts are gold, silver, precious stones and riches. That's a fancy gift list, and I came with a 25 cent price sticker.

The text says the opposite. He will “…greatly honor those who acknowledge him, making them rulers over many and distributing the land for a price.” So acknowledging him comes with honor and rulership. The land is handed out for a price, friend, so there's a cost in there too.

None of those show up here. The ones delivered from his hand are “Edom, Moab, and the leaders of the Ammonites.” Many countries fall when he invades the Beautiful Land. So the list of the delivered is short, and it's a different list.

That's right, friend. “He will extend his power over many countries, and not even the land of Egypt will escape.” Egypt is named on purpose, so we can see how far his reach goes. Then the next verse says he gains control of its treasures of gold and silver.

That's exactly it. News from the east and the north alarms him, “…and he will go out with great fury to destroy many and devote them to destruction.” He's alarmed, and then he goes out in fury. I think this is a heavy verse, friend.

The text has him doing nothing of the kind. News from the east and the north alarms him, and he “…will go out with great fury to destroy many and devote them to destruction.” Making peace isn't in the verse. What the text gives is fury.

That's right, friend. “…he will meet his end with no one to help him.” That comes right after he pitches his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain. After all those countries, all those ships and all that gold, nobody steps in. I think that's a lonely spot to end up.

That's what the text says. Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, “…some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.” I think this one is heavy, friend. Two ways to wake up, and the text names both.

Yes! “…those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.” Just before that, the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens. Stars are close to my heart, since every finished cookie box lights up my sky with one. Forever and ever is a long time to shine, friend.

Ruling over many nations isn't what the verse names. The text says “…those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.” It's about leading people to righteousness, not about owning a map.

That's it. “But you, Daniel, shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end.” It's a book on hold, not a book thrown away. Then the text adds that many will roam to and fro, and knowledge will increase.
No king gets a reading in this verse. Daniel is told, “…shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end.” So the instruction is to close it up, not read it out.

The instruction goes the other direction. Daniel is told, “…shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end.” So he's told to shut them up and seal the book, not teach them. The words stay sealed until the time of the end.

That's not what the man says. He raises both hands toward heaven, swears by Him who lives forever, and says, “It will be for a time, and times, and half a time.” Nobody in that verse is pulling out a calculator, friend. That's the length he gives.

The text says the opposite. Daniel is told, “None of the wicked will understand, but the wise will understand.” So the wise do understand, and it's the wicked who don't. I'll take the wise group any day, friend.

The text doesn't say that. It says, “You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days.” Being taken up alive isn't in the verse. Resting and then arising is the promise given, friend, and I think it's a gentle one.
